extracted.intended_audience: aspiring poets, describers, and literary readers interested in how to affect the imagination
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative criteria for producing descriptions, poetic imagery, and architectonic/landscape depictions that affect the reader's imagination; includes what pleases the fancy, how to use words, and how to cultivate the imagination. Geared toward poets and literary craftsmen.

rubrics_metrics.name: What pleases the imagination: Great, Uncommon, or Beautiful
rubrics_metrics.description: There is nothing in this whole Art which pleases the Imagination, but as it is Great, Uncommon, or Beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming to affect the imagination, ensure the object or description presents greatness, novelty/strangeness, or beauty; these are the primary virtues that excite the reader's fancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greatness in architecture: bulk versus manner
rubrics_metrics.description: Greatness may relate to the Bulk and Body of the Structure, or to the Manner in which it is built.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A small building with a great manner can give nobler ideas than a much larger one with an ordinary manner (example: Pantheon versus a larger Gothic cathedral). Consider both scale and the manner of execution when designing or describing architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grandeur of manner: few large principal members, avoid small ornamental confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: To introduce into Architecture this Grandeur of Manner,... the Division of the Principal Members of the Order may consist but of few Parts, that they be all great and of a bold and ample Relievo,... the Imagination may be more vigorously touched.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor large, bold primary members and projections; avoid redundancy of small ornaments that divide the eye into many rays (e.g., excessive quarter rounds, intermingled particulars). Use examples like a cornice where too many small parts harm the solemn effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of concave and convex forms (round pillars, vaults, domes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Among all the Figures in Architecture, there are none that have a greater Air than the Concave and the Convex... round Pillars and Vaulted Roofs make a great Part of those Buildings which are designed for Pomp and Magnificence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer curved, continuous surfaces (domes, arches, round pillars) when you want a magnificent, unified impression because the eye can take in more of the surface at once; arches and domes give a single, collected idea unlike square, faceted forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary pleasures: words can give more lively ideas than sight
rubrics_metrics.description: Words, when well chosen, have so great a Force in them, that a Description often gives us more lively Ideas than the Sight of Things themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use description to select, enlarge, and combine parts of a scene so the reader's imagination receives a fuller, sometimes superior, impression than direct observation. A poet may highlight aspects out of sight or combine seasonal beauties to intensify effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative principle: pleasure from comparing ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The Pleasure... proceeds from that Action of the Mind, which compares the Ideas that arise from Words, with the Ideas that arise from the Objects themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design descriptions and verbal representations to invite comparison (resemblance, analogy, contrast). Wit, mimickry, and many pleasant entertainments arise from perceived affinity or congruity between ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of words: force, significance, and expressive conjunction
rubrics_metrics.description: A Man should... have well weighed the Force and Energy that lye in the several Words of a Language, so as to be able to distinguish which are most significant and expressive of their proper Ideas, and what additional Strength and Beauty they are capable of receiving from Conjunction with others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate a fine sense of lexical force and collocation; select words that most precisely and powerfully evoke the intended ideas. Differences in readers' relish often come from their capacity to perceive these verbal energies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate imagination and judgment together
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fancy must be warm to retain the Print of those Images... and the Judgment discerning, to know what Expressions are most proper to cloath and adorn them to the best Advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both a lively imaginative capacity and a discriminating judgment are required: train the fancy by observation and reading, and temper it with critical sense so descriptions are vivid without being indiscriminate or clumsy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Store the mind with varied images (country, court, art)
rubrics_metrics.description: He must gain a due Relish of the Works of Nature, and be thoroughly conversant in the various Scenary of a Country Life... if he would go beyond Pastoral, and the lower kinds of Poetry, he ought to acquaint himself with the Pomp and Magnificence of courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read widely and observe varied scenes (rural life, courtly pomp, painting, statuary, architecture). A broad repertoire of images lets the poet choose the appropriate register (great, beautiful, strange) for any effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match poetic model to intended effect (Homer, Virgil, Ovid, Milton examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Homer strikes the Imagination with what is Great, Virgil with what is Beautiful, and Ovid with what is Strange... Milton may pass for a master in all these Arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing, consciously adopt models or techniques suited to your aim: epic sublimity, ordered beauty, or strange novelty. Study exemplar poets to learn how they generate specific imaginative effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of terror and pity (safe distance reflection) to produce pleasurable emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: The two leading Passions... are Terror and Pity... we are delighted with reflecting upon Dangers that are past, or in looking on a Precipice at a distance,... because we consider them as Dreadful and Harmless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evoking fear or sorrow can be pleasurable when the reader can reflect safely; craft distance, fictional status, or past-tense framing so the audience can admire the terror without being personally endangered, allowing reflection on one's own safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptions may improve on nature but must avoid absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: He has the modelling of Nature in his own Hands, and may give her what Charms he pleases, provided he does not reform her too much, and run into Absurdities, by endeavouring to excel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feel free to rearrange or intensify natural features (blend seasons, combine flowers, alter topography) to heighten delight, but maintain internal plausibility; avoid combinations that strike the reader as impossible or absurd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trigger associative sets: single particulars should awaken whole scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Any single Circumstance... often raises up a whole Scene of Imagery, and awakens numberless Ideas that before slept in the Imagination; such a particular Smell or Colour is able to fill the Mind... with the Picture of the Fields or Gardens, where we first met with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use evocative particulars (smell, color, a single object) to activate associative memory chains; specific sensory hints can blow up an entire prospect in the reader's mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: The 'fairy way' requires a particular cast of fancy and traditional knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a kind of Writing... Fairies, Witches, Magicians, Demons... more difficult... because he has no Pattern to follow... he ought to be very well versed in Legends and Fables, antiquated Romances, and the Traditions of Nurses and old Women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To create convincing supernatural or wholly-invented beings, cultivate a naturally fertile, superstitious imagination and learn folk traditions and legends; render such beings' speech and thought slightly 'discoloured' (not merely ordinary human) to make them distinct and credible.
